title: Replicating a published 49%-a-year stat-arb
hypothesis: Graph-clustered intra-cluster reversal (SPONGE + classifier) earns the published return.
question: A 2024 paper reported 49% a year from clustering S&P 500 stocks with a signed-graph method and trading short-term reversals inside each cluster. Does it replicate, and where does the return go when each assumption is moved to realistic conditions?
prior: Red flags before we started: positions opened and closed at the same close that generated the signal; no slippage; parameters swept over the test period; and growth attributed to two tickers that were later reused by different companies.
citations: Korniejczuk, A. & Ślepaczuk, R. (2024). Statistical arbitrage in multi-pair trading strategy based on graph clustering algorithms in US equities market. arXiv 2406.10695.
Cucuringu, M., Davies, P., Glielmo, A. & Tyagi, H. (2019). SPONGE: A generalized eigenproblem for clustering signed networks. AISTATS.
Cartea, Á., Cucuringu, M. & Jin, Q. (2023). Correlation Matrix Clustering for Statistical Arbitrage Portfolios. ICAIF.
method: One change per step: paper headline (R1) → clean prices (R2) → next-open fills at 7 bps (R3) → walk-forward classifier (R4); plus a simpler benchmark under paper (C0) and realistic (C0h) conditions.
Seven sensitivity runs on R4; trial count 38 fixed in advance (39 with one pre-registered diagnostic).
Data limit: our S&P OHLC cache starts 2011-09, so the test period is 2017-09 → 2026-09, not the paper's 2006–2022.
verdict_reason: It did not replicate. With the paper's own settings (same-close fills, 5 bps, raw prices, a classifier trained once) it made −0.3% a year, Sharpe −0.18, over 2017–2026, and traded on only 4 of 228 rebalances. With clean prices, next-morning fills at 7 bps and a walk-forward classifier (R4) it never traded at all: the classifier almost never scored a short signal above its 0.6 threshold, and the strategy needs a long and a short leg. Hedging the long side with SPY instead (a pre-registered diagnostic) lost 12.5% a year. Every pre-registered criterion failed.
lessons: Same-close execution and parameter sweeps on the test period can manufacture a headline; one change at a time shows where the return goes.
Check what a price series is before trusting it: the paper's two best tickers were later companies trading under symbols reused from old S&P members.
A market-neutral rule that needs both legs is fragile when a classifier learns the market's drift and stops trusting one side.
Our S&P price cache starts in 2011, so we tested 2017–2026 rather than the paper's 2006–2022.
